titleEn: The Song of the Cid — Alcocer sold; camp on the hill by Monreal; the king half-pardons Minaya (tiradas 44–48, lines 836–898)
part: Tiradas 44–48 · Alcocer sold; camp on the hill by Monreal; the king half-pardons Minaya (lines 836–898)

sentences.t:
Ya es aguisado, mañánas f[o] Minaya,
e el Campeador [fincó y] con su mesnada.
sentences.l:
Already it-is arranged, in-the-morning went Minaya,
and the Campeador [stayed there] with his company.
sentences.i: All is now made ready: in the morning Minaya was gone, and the Campeador stayed on there with his company.
sentences.n: Tirada 44 (assonance á-a) — the Çid sells Alcocer to the Moors (Pidal: El Cid vende Alcocer a los moros). The line-ends go back to á-a (Minaya, mesnada, mala, plata). aguisado, 'arranged, made ready' (aguisar, from guisa). mañánas, 'in the morning', an adverb with the adverbial -s (compare modern antes, entonces); the accent on the second a is printed so by Pidal and kept as printed, though it is unexpected. Pidal glosses the line 'por la mañana se fué Minaya', 'in the morning Minaya went off', and refers back to v. 827, where the horses were fed at nightfall. f[o] = fue, 'went' (fo, old preterite shared by ir and ser); the o is in italics: Pidal's restoration. fincó y, 'stayed there' (fincar, 'to remain', f- for modern h-; y = allí, 'there'): both words are printed in italics, supplied by Pidal. mesnada, 'household troop, company'.

sentences.t: La tierra es angosta e sobejana de mala.
sentences.l: The land is narrow and excessive of bad.
sentences.i: The land is cramped and wretched beyond measure.
sentences.n: angosta, 'narrow', and so 'poor, scanty', as the Çid said at v. 835. sobejana, 'excessive, beyond measure' (sobejo, 'surplus'); sobejana de mala, literally 'excessive in badness', i.e. exceedingly bad. The tenses now shift freely between present and past, as usual in the poem.

sentences.i: Every day the Moors of the border country and certain foreign folk kept watch on my Çid; King Fáriz had recovered, and they took counsel with him.
sentences.n: aguardar, 'to watch, keep an eye on'; the subject, moros … e unas yentes extrañas, comes after the verb, in the next line. a mio Çid, the personal object marked by a. yentes = gentes, 'peoples'; extrañas, 'foreign, from elsewhere'. sanó, 'got well': Fáriz was the Moorish king wounded by the Çid in the battle before Alcocer (three blows at v. 760; he fled into Terrer, v. 773: tiradas 35–39). consejavan, 'took counsel' (consejarse = aconsejarse).

sentences.t:
Entre los de Teca e los de Ter[rer] la casa,
e los de Calatayut, que es mas ondrada,
así lo an asmado e metudo en carta:
vendido les a Alcoçer por tres mill marcos de plata.
sentences.l:
Between those of Teca and those of Ter[rer] the town,
and those of Calatayut, which is more honoured,
so it they-have reckoned and put in writ:
sold to-them has Alcoçer for three thousand marks of silver.
sentences.i: The men of Teca and those of the town of Terrer, and those of Calatayud, which is the more honoured place, have worked it out and set it down in writing: he has sold them Alcocer for three thousand marks of silver.
sentences.n: Entre … e … e, 'between … and … and': Pidal notes that entre is pleonastic beside the conjunction (see his note on v. 191), so in effect 'both … and'. Ter[rer] la casa: Pidal, 'la población de Terrer', 'the town of Terrer' (compare v. 1232); the letters rer are in italics, his restoration. Teca (Ateca), Terrer and Calatayud are towns on the Jalón near Alcocer. mas = más, unaccented as printed. asmado, 'reckoned, considered' (asmar, 'to judge, estimate'); metudo = metido, 'put', with the old participle in -udo. carta, 'written deed, document'. vendido les a = les ha vendido, 'he has sold them': the participle placed first, the auxiliary a (= ha, aver) after the pronoun. The subject, the Çid, is not named. marcos, 'marks', a weight of silver (about half a pound).

sentences.t:
Mio Çid Ruy Díaz a Alcoçer [ha] ven[d]ido;
qué bien pago a s[o]s vassallos mismos!
sentences.l:
My Çid Ruy Díaz Alcoçer [has] sold;
how well he-paid his vassals own!
sentences.i: My Çid Ruy Díaz has sold Alcocer; how well he paid his own vassals!
sentences.n: Tirada 45 (assonance í-o) — the sale of Alcocer, told again (Pidal: Venta de Alcocer. (Repetición.)). The assonance changes to í-o (vendido, mismos, ricos, mesquino, deliçio), and the minstrel retells in the new assonance what the last tirada told, a common device of the poem. [ha] ven[d]ido: the word ha and the d of vendido are in italics, Pidal's restorations. pago is printed without an accent; the sense is the preterite pagó, 'paid, rewarded' (compare v. 806, ¡Dios, qué bien pagó a todos sus vassallos), and pagar also means 'to satisfy'. s[o]s = sus, the o Pidal's. mismos, 'own, very' (his very vassals). The exclamation has only the closing !, as printed.

sentences.t:
A cavalleros e a peones fechos los ha ricos,
en todos los sos non fallariedes un mesquino.
sentences.l:
To knights and to foot-soldiers made them he-has rich,
among all the his-men not you-would-find a wretch.
sentences.i: Knights and foot-soldiers alike he has made rich; among all his men you would not find one pauper.
sentences.n: fechos los ha ricos, 'he has made them rich' (fecho = hecho, f- for h-; the participle placed first and agreeing with the object, as often). peones, 'foot-soldiers'. los sos, 'his men'. fallariedes = hallaríais, 'you would find', conditional of fallar with the old -iedes ending; the poet speaks to his listeners. mesquino, 'poor wretch' (from Arabic miskīn).

sentences.t: Qui a buen señor sirve, siempre bive en deliçio.
sentences.l: Who to good lord serves, always lives in delight.
sentences.i: He who serves a good lord lives ever in comfort.
sentences.n: Qui = quien, 'he who'. bive = vive. deliçio, 'delight, ease'. Pidal: this line is a proverb found with variants: 'quien a buen señor sirve, buen galardón alcanza' ('who serves a good lord wins a good reward'), 'quien a buen señor sirve, esse vive en bienandanza' ('who serves a good lord lives in good fortune'), etc.

sentences.t:
Quando mio Çid el castiello quiso quitar,
moros e moras tomáronse a quexar:
sentences.l:
When my Çid the castle wanted to-leave,
Moors and Mooresses took-themselves to lament:
sentences.i: When my Çid was ready to leave the castle, the Moors, men and women, began to lament:
sentences.n: Tirada 46 (assonance á) — Alcocer abandoned; good omens; the Çid settles on the Poyo above Monreal (Pidal: Abandono de Alcocer. Buenos agüeros. — El Cid se asienta en el Poyo sobre Monreal). The assonance is now a single stressed á (quitar, quexar, part, Bivar, llorar, va, cabadelant …). quitar, 'to leave, quit (a place)'. moros e moras, 'Moorish men and women', the Moorish townsfolk let back into the castle at v. 801. tomáronse a quexar, 'they took to lamenting' (tomarse a + infinitive, 'to begin to'; the se glued after the verb).

sentences.t:
“¿vaste, mio Çid; nuestras oraçiones váyante delante!
Nos pagados finca[mo]s, señor, de la tu part.”
sentences.l:
“You-go-away, my Çid; our prayers may-they-go-to-you before!
We satisfied we-remain, lord, of the thy part.”
sentences.i: “Are you going, my Çid? May our prayers go before you! We remain well content with you, lord.”
sentences.n: vaste = te vas, 'you go away' (vas + te, irse); Pidal prints ¿ at the start and closes the sentence with !, with a semicolon between, and the text keeps his punctuation. váyante delante, 'may they go before you' (subjunctive of ir + te). Nos, 'we', the subject pronoun, printed here without the accent Pidal gives nós in v. 896b. pagados, 'satisfied, content' (pagar, 'to please'). finca[mo]s, 'we remain' (fincar); the letters mo are in italics, Pidal's. de la tu part, 'with your side, with your dealings', i.e. you have treated us well; la tu, article + possessive. The townsfolk speak to the Çid with the familiar tú.

sentences.t:
Quando quitó a Alcoçer mio Çid el de Bivar,
moros e moras compeçaron de llorar.
sentences.l:
When left Alcoçer my Çid he of Bivar,
Moors and Mooresses began to weep.
sentences.i: When my Çid of Vivar left Alcocer, the Moors, men and women, began to weep.
sentences.n: quitó, 'left' (quitar, as v. 851); the tirada repeats its own opening, sharpening lament into weeping. el de Bivar, 'he of Vivar', the Çid's home. compeçaron = comenzaron, 'began' (compeçar de + infinitive). Pidal: on the good treatment the Çid gives the Moors, compare v. 802 and his introduction, p. 59, n. 1.

sentences.t:
Alçó su seña, el Campeador se va,
passó Salón ayuso, aguijó cabadelant,
al exir de Salón mucho ovo buenas aves.
sentences.l:
He-raised his banner, the Campeador himself goes,
passed Salón down-stream, spurred forward,
at-the going-out from Salón much had good birds.
sentences.i: He raised his banner and the Campeador is on his way; he went down along the Jalón and spurred onward; as he left the Jalón he had very good omens.
sentences.n: Alçó = alzó, 'raised'. seña, 'banner, standard'. se va, 'goes off', present beside the preterites (epic tense-mixing). Salón, the river Jalón; ayuso, 'down, downstream'. aguijó, 'spurred on' (aguijar, as at v. 10, 'to set spurs'). cabadelant = cab adelant, 'onward, forward' (cabo, 'end, head', + adelante). exir = salir, 'to go out' (compare exida, v. 11). ovo = hubo, 'had' (preterite of aver). buenas aves: Pidal, like Latin bona avis, it means 'good omens' (the birds seen on setting out; compare p. 18, n. 2 of his edition and the crow at vv. 11–12). aves ends in á-e: in an á tirada an unstressed final e does not count against the assonance.

sentences.t:
Plogo a los de Terrer e a los de Calatayut más,
pesó a los de Alcocer, ca pro les fazié grant.
sentences.l:
It-pleased those of Terrer and those of Calatayut more,
it-grieved those of Alcocer, for profit to-them he-was-doing great.
sentences.i: It pleased the men of Terrer, and those of Calatayud still more; it grieved the people of Alcocer, for he had done them great good.
sentences.n: Plogo = plugo, 'it pleased' (old preterite of plazer, placer). pesó, 'it grieved' (pesar, 'to weigh on'). Alcocer is printed here with plain c (Alcoçer elsewhere): kept as printed. ca, 'for'. pro, 'profit, advantage' (as in modern en pro de). fazié = hacía, 'was doing', the old imperfect in -ié (f- for h-).

sentences.i: My Çid spurred on and kept riding forward, and halted on a hill that stands above Monreal; high is the hill, wondrous and great; it fears no attack, I tell you, from any side.
sentences.n: ivas = íbase, 'he went off' (iva + se). y ffincó, 'there he stopped, pitched camp': y, 'there', as in v. 837 (it might also be read as 'and'); ffincó, fincar written with the scribe's doubled ff. poyo, 'hill, height'. Pidal: Mont Real is Monreal del Campo, on the river Jiloca, seventeen hours' journey from Calatayud; the hill is El Poyo, a village on the left of the Jiloca on the road from Sagunto to Calatayud (v. 644), commanded by a high poyo or hill whose summit stands 1227 metres above sea level; it was anciently called El Poyo de mio Cid, as the poet says at v. 902, which the Fuero de Molina confirms by naming El Poyo de mio Cit among the boundaries of that city. sabet = sabed, 'know' (imperative, a stock aside to the listeners). nulla = ninguna, 'no, any' (Latin nulla); a nulla part, 'from any side', with non … nulla a double negative.

sentences.t:
Metió en paria a D[a]roca enantes,
desí a Molina, que es del otra part,
la terçera Teruel, que estava delant;
en su mano tenié a Çelfa la del Canal.
sentences.l:
He-put in tribute D[a]roca before,
then Molina, which is of-the other side,
the third Teruel, which was in-front;
in his hand he-held Çelfa that of-the Canal.
sentences.i: He had earlier put Daroca under tribute, then Molina, which lies on the far side, and third Teruel, which lay ahead; he held Cella of the Canal in his hand.
sentences.n: Metió en paria, 'he put under tribute' (paria, the tribute a Moorish town paid for protection). D[a]roca, the a in italics, Pidal's. enantes, 'before, beforehand'. desí, 'then, after that'. la terçera, 'the third (town)'. tenié = tenía, 'held' (imperfect in -ié). Çelfa la del Canal, 'Çelfa, that of the Canal': Pidal, today Cella (see his note on v. 644). Pidal (in the same note on v. 864): El Poyo lies 10 km from Monreal, 35 from Daroca, 50 from Molina and from Cella, and 65 from Teruel; all were towns of the Muslim kingdom of Zaragoza.

sentences.i: My Çid Ruy Díaz, God's grace be on him! Minaya Álvar Fáñez has gone to Castile; the thirty horses he was presenting to the king;
sentences.n: Tirada 47 (assonance á-a) — Minaya comes before the King, who pardons Minaya but not the Çid (Pidal: Minaya llega ante el Rey. — Este perdona a Minaya, pero no al Cid). The line-ends return to á-a (graçia, Minaya, enpresentava, sonrrisava …). The scene moves from the Çid's camp to the king's court. R[o]y = Ruy, only the o in italics. aya = haya, 'may he have' (subjunctive of aver, a wish). Ido es, 'has gone' (ir forms its perfect with ser). Álbar Fáñez Minaya: the name with Minaya placed last, as printed. treynta = treinta. los enpresentava, 'he was presenting them' (enpresentar, 'to present as a gift'), the object thirty horses taken up again by los: the gift of vv. 815–818.

sentences.t:
ví[d]olos el rey, fermoso sonrrisava:
“¿quin los dio estos, si vos vala Dios, Minaya!”
sentences.l:
Saw-them the king, handsomely he-was-smiling:
“who them gave these, so you may-protect God, Minaya!”
sentences.i: The king saw them and smiled most graciously: “Who gave these, God keep you, Minaya?”
sentences.n: ví[d]olos = viólos, 'he saw them', from the old preterite vido; the d is in italics on the scan (checked at 600 dpi: the slanted stem and pointed top of the italic d, as in the wholly italic v. 875e, against the upright roman d of dio in the next line): Pidal's restoration. fermoso, 'handsomely, beautifully' (hermoso, f- for h-), an adjective used as an adverb. sonrrisava, 'was smiling', with the double rr as printed. quin = quién, 'who'. los … estos, 'them … these', the object said twice. si vos vala Dios, 'so may God protect you' (valer, 'to help, protect'), a courteous oath. Pidal opens with ¿ and closes with !, as printed.

sentences.t:
—“Mio Çid R[o]y Díaz, que en buen ora cinxo espada.
Pues quel vos ayrastes, Alcoçer gañó por maña;
sentences.l:
—“My Çid R[o]y Díaz, who in good hour girded sword.
Since-that-him you angered-at, Alcoçer he-won by craft;
sentences.i: “My Çid Ruy Díaz, who girded on his sword in a good hour. Since you turned your anger on him, he has won Alcocer by stratagem;
sentences.n: Minaya answers; the dash before the quotation mark is Pidal's. cinxo, 'girded', old strong preterite of ceñir; en buen ora, 'in a good hour', the epic formula. quel = que le, 'that … him' (pues que, 'since'). gañó = ganó, 'won', with ñ as printed (gañar beside ganar). ayrastes = airasteis, 'you angered at', i.e. withdrew your favour from him (the -astes ending of the 2nd plural preterite). maña, 'craft, stratagem': the feigned retreat by which the Çid took Alcocer. The line 875b and the three that follow (875c–875e) are printed wholly in italics by Pidal: they are his restoration, not the manuscript's, and are printed here in plain type; they have no numbers in his margin (his next number is 880), and the letters b–e are provisional numbers of ours.

sentences.t:
al rey de Valençia dello el mensaje llegava,
mandólo y çercar, e tolléronle el agua.
Mio Çid salió del castiello, en campo lidiava,
sentences.l:
to-the king of Valençia of-it the message was-coming,
he-ordered-him there to-besiege, and they-took-from-him the water.
My Çid went-out of-the castle, in field he-was-fighting,
sentences.i: word of it reached the king of Valencia, who had him besieged there, and they cut off his water. My Çid sallied from the castle and fought in the open field;
sentences.n: These three lines are Pidal's restoration (wholly italic in his print, unnumbered there; the letters c–e are ours). They sum up in a few words what the poem has already told at length: the king of Valencia sent his host against the Çid in Alcocer, the besiegers cut off the water, and the Çid broke out and won the battle in the field. dello = de ello, 'of it'. llegava, imperfect beside preterites (epic tense-mixing). mandólo y çercar, 'he had him besieged there' (lo, the Çid, as le in the next phrase; it could also be 'it', the place; y, 'there'). tolléronle el agua, 'they took the water from him' (toller, 'to take away', + le). lidiava, 'fought' (lidiar; lid, 'battle').

sentences.t:
venció dos reyes de moros en aquesta batalla,
sobejana es, señor, la su[e] ganançia.
sentences.l:
he-conquered two kings of Moors in this battle,
excessive is, lord, the his gain.
sentences.i: he defeated two Moorish kings in that battle; great beyond measure, my lord, is his gain.
sentences.n: From v. 876 the manuscript's own text resumes. The two kings are Fáriz and Galve (vv. 654 ff.). aquesta = esta. sobejana, 'exceeding great', as v. 838. la su[e] ganançia, 'his gain, his winnings', article + possessive; sue is an old feminine of the possessive (sua), the e in italics, Pidal's.

sentences.i: To you, honoured king, he sends this present; he kisses your feet and both your hands, and begs that you show him mercy, so may the Creator keep you.”
sentences.n: ondrado, 'honoured' (honrado). presentaja, 'present, gift'. bésavos, 'he kisses you' (besa + vos, the dative of the person). pie[de]s, the old plural piedes, 'feet', the letters de in italics, Pidal's. amas = ambas, 'both'. Pidal: besavos los piedes que …, 'he begs you to …' (compare v. 179): the kiss of feet and hands is the formula of a vassal's petition. quel = que le; ay[a]des = hayáis, 'you may have' (the a in italics): aver merçed de, 'to have mercy on, show favour to'. si el Criador vos vala, 'so may the Creator protect you'.

sentences.t:
Dixo el rey: “mucho es mañana,
omne ayrado, que de señor non ha graçia,
por acogello a cabo de tres se[d]manas.
sentences.l:
Said the king: “much it-is morning,
man angered-at, who of lord not has grace,
for to-take-him-back at end of three weeks.
sentences.i: The king said: “It is far too soon to take back, after three weeks, a man in disgrace who has lost his lord's favour.
sentences.n: Dixo = dijo, 'said'. mucho es mañana: Pidal, 'es muy pronto', 'it is very early, too soon'. omne ayrado, 'a man under the king's anger' (omne = hombre; ayrado, the formal disfavour that sent the Çid into exile); it is the object of acogello, placed first. ha = tiene, 'has' (aver). acogello = acogerlo, 'to receive him back' (the r of the infinitive assimilated to the l of the pronoun). a cabo de, 'at the end of'. se[d]manas = semanas, the d in italics, Pidal's. Pidal: tres sedmanas expresses a short, indefinite time; the winning and holding of Alcocer alone had taken eighteen weeks (vv. 573, 664), and we must suppose that five or six months of exile had passed when the king says these words.

sentences.t:
Mas después que de moros f[o], prendo esta presentaja;
aun me plaze de mio Çid que fizo tal ganançia.
sentences.l:
But since that from Moors it-was, I-take this present;
still to-me it-pleases of my Çid that he-made such gain.
sentences.i: But since it was taken from Moors, I accept this present; and I am glad besides of my Çid, that he has won such spoils.
sentences.n: f[o] = fue, 'it was', the o Pidal's; de moros fo, 'it came from Moors', i.e. it was won from the infidel, so the king can accept it without seeming to favour an exile. prendo, 'I take' (prender = tomar). In Pidal's print the last word, presentaja, does not fit on its line and is broken presen-, with the end taja set at the end of the line above after a bracket; here it is put back in its own line. aun, 'still, moreover'. plaze = place, 'it pleases'. fizo = hizo (f- for h-). ganançia, 'gain, booty'. The king speaks of mio Çid, using the hero's epithet himself.

sentences.t:
Sobresto todo, a vos quito Minaya,
honores e tierras avellas condonadas,
id e venit, d'aquí vos do mi graçia;
mas del Çid Campeador, yo non vos digo nada.
sentences.l:
Over-this all, to you I-absolve Minaya,
honours and lands have-them restored,
go and come, from-here to-you I-give my grace;
but of-the Çid Campeador, I not to-you I-say nothing.
sentences.i: Over and above all this, you, Minaya, I pardon; your honours and lands, take them back restored; go and come freely, from now on I give you my favour; but of the Çid Campeador I say nothing to you.
sentences.n: Sobresto = sobre esto, 'over and above this'. quito, 'I release, pardon' (quitar, 'to clear, free'). Pidal: honores e tierras (as at v. 3413) were the revenues and territories the king granted to a man in tenure or government; whoever received the tierra or the honor collected its rents, administered justice and had to keep a certain number of knights to serve the king in war three months a year. avellas = avedlas, 'have them' (imperative aved + las, the d assimilated). condonadas: Pidal, condonar, 'to grant, restore'; the king gives back to Minaya what he had confiscated from him for going with the Çid (compare vv. 230, 289, 893, 1363–64). venit = venid, 'come'. d'aquí, 'from here, from now'. do = doy, 'I give'. graçia, the king's favour. non vos digo nada, double negative: the Çid himself stays unpardoned.

sentences.t:
Sobre aquesto todo, dezir vos quiero, [Álbar Fáñez]:
de todo mio reyno los que lo quisieren far,
buenos e valientes pora mio Çid huyar,
suéltoles los cuerpos e quítoles las heredades.”
sentences.l:
Over this all, to-say to-you I-want, [Álbar Fáñez]:
of all my kingdom those who it may-wish to-do,
good and valiant, for my Çid to-help,
I-loose-to-them the bodies and I-clear-to-them the inheritances.”
sentences.i: Over and above all this, I wish to tell you, Álvar Fáñez: those from all my kingdom who may wish to do it, good and valiant men, to go to my Çid's aid — I set their persons free and leave their estates untouched.”
sentences.n: Tirada 48 (assonance á) — the King allows Castilians to go with the Çid (Pidal: El Rey permite a los castellanos irse con el Cid). The king's speech runs on, but the assonance changes to á (far, huyar, heredades, Fáñez, natural, adelant …); heredades and Fáñez end in á-e, the unstressed final e not counting. aquesto = esto. dezir vos quiero, 'I want to tell you'. [Álbar Fáñez]: the name is printed in italics, supplied by Pidal; on the scan the italic name has no accent on the A (Albar, against Álbar in roman at v. 894), so the pinned text's Á is not Pidal's here (left for the owner). quisieren, future subjunctive of querer. far, short form of fazer, 'to do'. pora = para. huyar, 'to help, come to the aid of': this is how the line is read here, from the context of the king's permission; the word is rare, Pidal has no footnote on it, and the reading is offered with caution. suéltoles los cuerpos, 'I release their persons' (they incur no penalty), and quítoles las heredades, 'I leave their estates free': Pidal, the king promises not to confiscate the inherited lands of those who go with the Çid (compare v. 887). The -les glued on the verbs is the enclitic dative.

sentences.i: Minaya Álvar Fáñez kissed his hands: “Thanks, and thanks again, my king, as to my natural lord; this you do now; the rest you will do hereafter; with God's help we shall so bear ourselves that you will do it.”
sentences.n: Besóle las manos, 'he kissed his hands' (le, the dative of the person), the vassal's gesture. Grado e graçias, 'thanks and thanks': Pidal, in his note on v. 792, cites this line for grado ('gratitude') beside its synonym graçias. señor natural, 'natural lord', the lord to whom one owes allegiance by birth. feches, 'you do' (a shortened form of fazedes). al, 'the rest, something else' (Latin aliud). feredes = haréis, 'you will do' (future of fer, fazer). adelant, 'hereafter'. Minaya asks, without saying it, that the king one day pardon the Çid too. The last line, 896b, is printed wholly in italics by Pidal: it is his restoration, printed here in plain type, and unnumbered in his margin; the letter b is ours. guisaremos, 'we will arrange, so act' (guisar); nós and vós, the stressed pronouns, accented as printed. fagades = hagáis (subjunctive of fazer).

sentences.t:
Dixo el rey: “Minaya, esso sea de vagar.
Id por Castiella e déxenvos andar,
si'nulla dubda id a mio Çid buscar.”
sentences.l:
Said the king: “Minaya, that may-be of leisure.
Go through Castiella and let-them-let-you go,
without-any fear go to my Çid to-seek.”
sentences.i: The king said: “Minaya, let that be for another day. Go through Castile, and let no one hinder you; without any fear go and seek my Çid.”
sentences.n: The first line, 896c, is printed wholly in italics by Pidal: his restoration, which supplies the king's reply; it is unnumbered in his margin, and the letter c is ours. esso sea de vagar, 'let that be at leisure', i.e. there is no hurry for that (vagar, 'leisure'). déxenvos andar, 'let them let you go about' (subjunctive of dexar + vos): no one is to stop him. si'nulla dubda = sin nulla dubda, 'without any fear', the apostrophe printed so by Pidal to mark the lost n; dubda, 'fear' as well as 'doubt' (see v. 786). id a mio Çid buscar, 'go and seek my Çid' (ir a + infinitive, the object placed between). The king himself again says mio Çid.
